notes.h: What HACCP is and the terms it uses (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Rather than waiting to test finished food, a food business can look for trouble at every step and stop it early. That is the idea behind HACCP, and it comes with a small set of terms that exams ask you to define.
points: HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point. It is a preventive system, which means it identifies and controls hazards at each stage from raw material to consumer, before they can reach the consumer, rather than relying on testing the finished product.

A hazard is anything that could contaminate food or harm the consumer. A control measure is an action that prevents, removes or reduces a hazard, such as thorough cooking, which destroys surviving bacteria.

A critical control point (CCP) is a step at which a control measure is essential and can be monitored, for example the cooking step. A critical limit is the value that separates safe from unsafe, for example a minimum core temperature.
Hazard analysis identifies the hazards at each stage of food processing and assesses how likely and how serious each one is, so effort goes where the risk is greatest.
HACCP is used by caterers, restaurants, food manufacturers and food businesses generally.
notes.tip: A critical control point is a step, while a critical limit is a value. Do not mix them up. When asked for a hazard and a control measure, give both as a pair with an example each, because a hazard alone or a control alone earns only half.

notes.h: Three types of hazard (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Hazards fall into three groups depending on what the contaminant is. Naming the type, with an example, helps you decide what control measure fits.
points: Biological hazards are micro-organisms, such as food poisoning bacteria, moulds and viruses, which can multiply in food and make people ill.
Chemical hazards include pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals, metal residues and allergens, which can get into food during growing, cleaning or processing.
Physical hazards are foreign bodies such as glass, metal, bone, stones, pests and hair, which can injure the consumer or signal poor hygiene.

notes.h: The seven principles of HACCP (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The seven principles are the steps a business follows to build a HACCP system. They run in a logical order: find the hazards, pick the key steps, set limits, check them, fix problems, prove it works and write it all down.
points: Principle 1: carry out a hazard analysis at each stage of the process.
Principle 2: identify the critical control points, the steps where control is essential.
Principle 3: set a critical limit for each critical control point, such as a minimum cooking temperature.
Principle 4: set up monitoring procedures to check each critical control point, so you know the limit is being met.
Principle 5: set corrective actions to take when monitoring shows that a critical limit has not been met.
Principle 6: set up verification procedures to confirm that the system is working.
Principle 7: keep records and documentation of the system and its results, which gives written evidence of what was done.
notes.tip: When asked to describe the stages of a HACCP system for a dish, follow the dish's journey from purchase to reheating, not this list of seven principles. Review of the system belongs to verification (principle 6), so do not add an eighth principle.

notes.h: Purchase, transport and storage of a hot main course (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A HACCP answer follows the food from the shop to the plate, giving a hazard and its control at each stage. The first three stages happen before any cooking starts.
points: Purchase hazards: damaged goods, bacterial or chemical contamination, and pests.

Purchase controls: buy from a reputable shop, and check packaging, use-by dates, temperatures and any signs of pest damage, so unsafe food is never brought home. Keep raw and cooked foods separate in the trolley, and choose foods within date and with quality assurance marks.
Transport hazard: bacteria multiply when food warms up during transport and delays, because warmth lets them grow quickly.
Transport control: carry perishable food in cool bags or refrigerated containers, cover it, minimise the time before it is stored, and store it promptly.
Storage hazards: bacterial multiplication and cross-contamination (bacteria passing from one food to another) of food.

Storage controls: chill perishable food below 5°C, freeze food at −18°C, and keep raw food separate from cooked food, with raw below cooked and covered. Check vegetables for mould, and use clean sealed containers.
notes.tip: Examiners expect six or so stages, each with a hazard and its control. Pair every hazard with a control, and make sure you refer to preparation and to cooking.

notes.h: Preparation and cooking of a hot main course (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Preparation and cooking are where food is handled most and where bacteria can be destroyed. Cooking is the critical control point, because it is the step that kills bacteria already on the food.
points: Preparation hazards: contamination of food, multiplication of bacteria and cross-contamination.

Preparation controls: wash hands with antibacterial soap and hot water before and after handling food, and handle food as little as possible. Keep perishables chilled until needed, and clean equipment in hot water and detergent.

Use colour-coded boards and separate utensils for raw and cooked meat, and keep raw meat away from cooked meat and ready-to-eat foods, so bacteria from raw meat cannot reach food that will not be cooked again.

Thaw frozen meat or poultry fully, preferably in the fridge on the bottom shelf, before cooking it. Thawing fully matters because a frozen centre may stay too cool to cook through, and the bottom shelf stops drips reaching other food.
Cooking hazard: bacteria that survive cooking, which can cause food poisoning.
Cooking control: cook thoroughly, turning or stirring the food regularly so that it cooks evenly, and use a thermometer to check.

Poultry must reach a core temperature (the temperature at the centre) of at least 72°C to destroy bacteria. In the exam example this is the critical limit, and the current FSAI guidance of 75°C is also correct.
notes.tip: A thermometer reading is the monitoring step, and the core temperature is the critical limit. Either 72°C or the current FSAI figure of 75°C is accepted for poultry.

notes.h: Serving and reheating a hot main course (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Safe cooking can be undone if food is left standing or reheated badly. The last two stages deal with bacteria that survived cooking and the food that is left over.
points: Serving hazards: surviving bacteria multiplying in food that is held too long, and cross-contamination from utensils.
Serving controls: serve cooked food straight after cooking, on a clean plate, with clean utensils.
Hold cooked food above 63°C, because bacteria multiply more slowly when it is kept hot, and do not hold it for more than about 90 minutes.
Reheating hazard: food that has been cooled and stored can have bacteria that multiply during storage, or survive.

Reheating control: cool leftovers quickly, cover them and refrigerate. Then reheat food quickly to above 100°C throughout, and reheat it only once. Current guidance of piping hot, about 70 to 75°C at the core, is also correct.

notes.h: A barbecue as a second example (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Exams can ask for the HACCP stages of a dish other than a hot main course, such as a barbecue. The stages are the same, with a few extra controls suited to outdoor cooking.
points: Cook poultry and sausages right through, with no pink or red juices, because pink juices show the centre has not reached a safe temperature.
Do not use the same plate or tongs for raw and cooked food, so raw-meat bacteria cannot pass onto food that is ready to eat.
Keep raw meat separate from salads, which will not be cooked, and keep perishable salads and coleslaw in the fridge until needed.
A marinade used on raw meat must be brought to the boil before it is used as a sauce, otherwise it carries raw-meat bacteria.

notes.b: HACCP helps both the consumer and the business. It makes food safer and gives the business proof that it took proper care.
points: HACCP identifies and eliminates or reduces hazards, so food is safer and outbreaks are prevented.
It focuses workers on safety at every step of food preparation.
It meets legal requirements and provides written records as evidence of due care.
Records help a business plan for future safety, time and cost, with less waste and fewer recalls.
It increases consumer confidence, and the system should be reviewed and evaluated regularly.
In a catering business, HACCP helps prevent food poisoning outbreaks by identifying hazards from purchase to serving, controlling them at critical points and monitoring to prevent contamination.
notes.tip: Questions ask for about three benefits, or for how HACCP helps a catering business prevent food poisoning. For the second, link hazards found from purchase to serving, control at critical points, monitoring, and regular review and evaluation.

notes.b: HACCP is not the only system a food business may use. ISO 9000 is a separate, broader approach to managing quality.
points: ISO is the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes internationally agreed standards. In Ireland the National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) is the national standards body.

ISO 9000 is a family of standards for quality management systems. A quality management system uses documented procedures, records and regular internal review to ensure that products meet customer requirements.
Continual improvement of the system is a central principle of ISO 9000.

ISO 9001 is the standard in the family against which organisations are formally audited and certified. Certification by an independent body shows customers that the business has a consistent quality system.
HACCP is a food safety system that controls hazards, whereas ISO 9000 is a general quality management system for any business and covers safety only indirectly. A food business can use both.
notes.tip: ISO 9000 is a quality management standard for any organisation, not a food safety standard, and it is not part of HACCP.

keyTerms.definition: A preventive food safety system that identifies hazards in food processing and controls them at critical points.
Anything that could contaminate food or harm the consumer, including micro-organisms, chemicals and foreign bodies.
The identification of hazards at each stage of food processing, and an assessment of how likely and how serious each one is.
An action that prevents, removes or reduces a hazard, such as thorough cooking or chilling.
A step in food processing at which a control measure is essential and can be monitored.
The maximum or minimum value, such as a cooking temperature, that a critical control point must meet to keep food safe.
The action taken when monitoring shows that a critical limit has not been met.
Checks, such as reviews and tests, that confirm a HACCP system is working as planned.
A family of international standards for quality management systems, published by the International Organization for Standardization.
A system of documented procedures, records and reviews used by an organisation to make sure its products meet requirements.

factCards.definition: Biological (bacteria and moulds), chemical (pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals and metal residues) and physical (glass, metal and bone).
Hazard analysis; identifying critical control points; setting critical limits; monitoring; corrective actions; verification; and records and documentation.
It eliminates or reduces hazards and produces safer food; it focuses workers on safety; and it fulfils legal requirements and provides records as evidence.

questions.prompt: Name the three types of hazard that can contaminate food, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Biological hazard: food poisoning bacteria such as Salmonella, or moulds. Chemical hazard: pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals or metal residues. Physical hazard: foreign bodies such as glass, metal or bone.

questions.prompt: Outline the stages of a HACCP system for making and serving a hot main course, identifying a hazard and a corresponding control measure at each stage.
questions.model: Purchase: hazards are damaged goods, contamination and pests; controls are buying from a reputable shop, checking packaging, dates, temperatures and pest damage. Transport and storage: hazards are bacterial growth and cross-contamination; controls are cool bags, minimal delay, covered food, chilling below 5°C and freezing at −18°C. Preparation: hazards are contamination, bacterial multiplication and cross-contamination; controls are handwashing, colour-coded boards, separate utensils for raw and cooked food, and fully thawing food in the fridge. Cooking: hazard is bacteria surviving cooking; control is thorough cooking with poultry reaching at least 72°C in the centre, turning food regularly. Serving and reheating: hazards are multiplication of surviving bacteria and cross-contamination from utensils; controls are serving on clean plates, holding food above 63°C for no more than about 90 minutes, and reheating quickly to above 100°C only once.
